text: Submitting a circuit to real hardware costs queue time and, often, money. Estimating qubit count, circuit depth, and total shot budget before submission lets you catch an infeasible or needlessly expensive job while it's still cheap to fix.

This lesson covers estimating the number of oracle calls Grover's search needs, estimating total shot budget for a variational algorithm's full training run, how circuit depth and qubit count together determine feasibility, and a resource-estimation checklist to run before any real-hardware submission.

Grover's search on N equals two to the n items needs approximately pi over four times the square root of N oracle calls to find a marked item with high probability. For ten qubits, that's 1024 items, giving roughly 25.13 iterations, verified directly — so you'd plan for 25 oracle calls. That single number has real consequences before you submit anything: if each oracle call requires around 40 two-qubit gates, the full circuit depth is roughly a thousand two-qubit-gate-equivalents before even counting the diffuser, a number worth checking against your backend's realistic noise-tolerant depth before submission.

A QAOA circuit with three layers has six variational parameters. Using the parameter-shift rule, each parameter needs two circuit evaluations, giving twelve circuit executions per gradient step. Over 100 optimizer iterations at 2000 shots per evaluation, that's 1,200 total circuit executions and 2.4 million total shots — verified by direct computation. That's the number that actually determines queue cost and runtime, not 'one circuit, 2000 shots,' which wildly understates what a full training run requires.

Resource estimation isn't only about shot budget — depth and qubit count determine whether a circuit is even feasible before accounting for noise. A circuit whose depth would take meaningfully longer to execute than a backend's coherence time is likely to produce results dominated by noise rather than signal, regardless of shot count. Checking qubit count against a backend's actual qubit count is the more basic check, and should be caught by an estimation step long before submission, not discovered from an error message after.

Before submitting any circuit to a real backend: confirm required qubits fit the backend, check estimated depth against the backend's realistic noise-tolerant depth, calculate the total shot budget for the entire run including any gradient-evaluation multiplier, and sanity-check the estimate against measured profiling data from a smaller prior run if one exists — far more trustworthy than a theoretical estimate alone. Next lesson is a hands-on lab putting profiling and estimation together to make an actual go or no-go call on a real-hardware run.
